Six hundred people applied for every watch. Not one of them stood on a pavement to do it.

Swatch allocated the 1,969 MoonSwatch Mission to the Moon 1969 pieces through the Electronic Swatch Timepiece Application, a 32-question online form. More than 1.2 million people completed it. The ticket is $570, a number Swatch took from the gold price on 21 July 1969 rather than from today, and JCK reports 11 grams of 18-karat gold across the dial, hands, crown and pushers.

That metal claim inverts the usual accounting. Eleven grams of 18-karat is 8.25 grams of fine gold, and at Tuesday's Kitco spot of $4,048.80 an ounce the fine content alone is worth about $1,074, close to twice the ticket. Swatch is not selling a margin on materials. It is selling a date.

The contrast is three months old. The Royal Pop collaboration with Audemars Piguet in May needed police outside stores in New York, Paris and London, closed 15 American shops on a Saturday, and traded at four to five times retail within days. JCK reports the same watch changing hands below $400 by August.

The form is the part most of the coverage missed. Thirty-two questions answered 1.2 million times is a verified database of watch buyers, their tastes and their intent, acquired at no cost against 1,969 units of inventory. The allocation problem was solved with a web page, and the byproduct is worth more than the run.

Thirteen months of decline ended in July, and it ended level. That is not the same as a recovery, and the difference is worth inventory.

The RapNet Diamond Index for 1-carat polished was unchanged across the month on figures Rapaport published on Tuesday. The three other headline sizes moved up: 0.30-carat gained 1.6%, 0.50-carat gained 1.8% and 3-carat gained 0.2%. It is the first month since March 2025 in which none of the four fell, which makes July the best month for polished since the April 2025 tariff schedule started rearranging where a stone can profitably be cut.

The 0.50-carat print is the one to mark. At 1.8% it is that size's largest monthly gain since March 2025, and it belongs to the band the American engagement counter actually clears. A recovery led by 0.30-carat goods with the 1-carat still falling is a mix shift. A recovery in which the 1-carat holds is a floor.

The trade should be honest about the other half. The schedule in force since late July keeps 10% on polished finished in India while loose natural diamonds cut in Belgium, Botswana and Namibia clear at zero. An index measured in dollars will reflect that gap before it reflects any change in what a buyer wants, and nobody currently publishes a series that separates the two.

What is unrepaired is still the larger picture. Lab-grown continues to take the entry price point, Chinese demand is weak on the tonnage series, and Rapaport reports American buying concentrated in 2-carat rounds, G to J, VS1 to SI2. That is a narrow lane rather than a broad bid.

A group of workshops that between them build a few thousand watches a year now clears more second-hand value than LVMH's entire watch portfolio.

EveryWatch, which compiles sold prices from about 650 dealers and roughly 470 auction houses, put global secondary transactions at $10.5 billion for the first half, up 37.2%, in a report published on 30 July. The median watch sold for $5,900, up 19%, and took 43 days against 39 a year ago. Value grew faster than volume, so the money moved up the ladder rather than across more wrists.

Independent makers took $633.8 million of that, up 89%. The LVMH watch portfolio transacted about $617 million over the same period. Nothing in the number says LVMH is shrinking. It says resale has stopped paying for brand scale.

Almost all the independent growth carries one name. F.P. Journe transacted $201.6 million, close to triple the prior year, which puts the 27-year-old Geneva house seventh among all watch brands by secondary value. Its median sale price rose 82% to $215,000 and its turnover rate ran above 57%, so more than half the Journe watches offered found a buyer while the price was still climbing. Behind it the field is small: H. Moser at $26 million, Parmigiani Fleurier at $21 million, De Bethune at $19 million.

Scale still sits where it always has. Rolex accounted for $4.29 billion, about 41% of all secondary value, and its certified pre-owned programme alone did $385 million, more than double the prior year. Geography split as sharply as brand: the United States and Canada transacted $4.5 billion, up 70%, while Asia fell 2.6%.
